items.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013
items.q: And Billy Taylor was probably it for the thirty years before anybody was a doctorate in music.

ctx.x: Yeah. And I did go to faculty meetings when it was really important for me to do that, but he really protected me. He buffered me from all the other stuff. And I didn’t know how much he had done until I began to go to other schools and be an artist-in-residence, and the guy said, “Man I’m so tired, I’ve been up all night with all my administrative stuff and I haven’t been able to do this and that.” And then he made it also, because our

program became really visible, he made it such that if another university was going to hire a jazz musician who had notoriety, they had to let them continue to be who they were, because that’s why they wanted them. So I would tell people, I said, “Well listen, if they want you to be who you are, then they’re going to have to give you some leeway to go out to travel to continue to do what you do.” Now there is a price for everything. So I mean I had to kind of, I couldn’t fly off just — because I was being paid,…

because I feel that it’s important that young people see. And I propelled them. I said, “just because you can play up and down your horn and play a lot of notes, that’s not enough. Never has been.” But Marty Krivin, and we are thankful to him that we got a chance to know he and JoAnn, because they made our whole lives change for the better.
